questions.question: According to the text, what is the defining requirement for a function to be considered "pure" in functional programming?

choices.statement: It must use loops instead of recursion
Its output value must depend only on the arguments that are input, so calling it twice with the same argument always produces the same result
It must modify a global variable to track its state
It must be written using object-oriented syntax

questions.hint: Same input, same output, every time.

questions.question: Functional programming's theoretical roots trace back to a formal system developed in the 1930s by Alonzo Church. What is this system called?

choices.statement: Turing machine
Lambda calculus
Relational algebra
Finite automaton

questions.hint: A formal system by Alonzo Church, named after a Greek letter.

questions.question: In mathematics, a function f is described as being defined "over" two sets. What are these two sets called, and which one contains the function's actual, guaranteed possible outputs plus any extra elements?

choices.statement: Domain and range; the range is the extra-elements set
Domain and codomain; the codomain is the set that contains the outputs plus possibly additional elements
Argument and image; the argument set contains extra elements
Input and graph; the graph contains extra elements

questions.hint: One set holds the inputs; the other holds the outputs and possibly more.

questions.question: A function is described in the text as "bijective" when it satisfies which condition?

choices.statement: It is neither injective nor surjective
It is injective (one-to-one) only
It is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto)
It has no inverse function

questions.hint: It has both properties at once: no repeats and nothing left out.

questions.question: In lambda calculus, what determines whether an occurrence of a variable within an expression is considered "bound" versus "free"?

choices.statement: A bound variable is one that is not declared anywhere in the expression, while a free variable is declared
A bound variable appears within the scope of a lambda abstraction (binding operator) for that variable; a free variable is not declared/bound in the expression
Bound and free refer only to whether the variable is capitalized
There is no distinction between bound and free variables in lambda calculus

questions.hint: Look at whether the variable sits inside the scope of a lambda that names it.

questions.question: What does the concept of "confluence" guarantee about lambda calculus reduction, according to the text?

choices.statement: Every expression can be reduced to multiple different normal forms depending on evaluation order
If an expression can be reduced to a normal form, that normal form is unique, regardless of the order in which subexpressions are evaluated
Expressions can never reach a normal form
Confluence only applies to imperative programming languages

questions.hint: The order of evaluation should not change the final result.

questions.question: In Java, the final keyword is used with primitive type variables. Based on the text's example, what exactly does final accomplish?

choices.statement: It makes the object referenced by the variable fully immutable, including all of its internal fields
It prevents the variable itself from being reassigned after it is defined, but for reference types it only prevents reassignment of the reference, not changes to the object's internal state
It converts the variable into a global variable automatically
It has no effect on primitive types, only on objects

questions.hint: final locks the variable itself, not necessarily everything it points to.

questions.question: What is a "closure," and how does it differ from an ordinary lambda function according to the text?

choices.statement: A closure is identical to a lambda; there is no difference
A closure is a function that can only be called once, while a lambda can be called many times

A closure references variables from outside its own scope (non-local variables) and must persist a representation of its lexical environment so those variables remain accessible even after the enclosing function returns
A closure can never take any parameters, unlike a lambda

questions.hint: A closure carries its surrounding environment along with it.

questions.question: What is "currying," as described in the text's C# and F# examples?

choices.statement: A technique for converting a function that accepts multiple parameters into a sequence of functions, each accepting only one parameter and returning the next function in the sequence
A method for removing all parameters from a function
A way to make a function execute in parallel across multiple threads
A technique exclusive to object-oriented programming that has no relation to functional programming

questions.hint: One function with many parameters becomes a chain of one-parameter functions.

questions.question: Why does the text emphasize that recursive functions should be written to be "tail recursive," using an accumulator argument (as in the tailpow example)?

choices.statement: Tail recursion has no practical benefit and is purely a stylistic choice
Without tail recursion, the function cannot return any value at all

Tail call elimination allows the stack to be reused (no need to remember the calling location), preventing the call stack from being exhausted on large inputs, since a non-tail-recursive call must still perform work after the recursive call returns
Tail recursion converts the function into an iterative loop automatically in every language

questions.hint: When the recursive call is the very last thing done, the stack can be reused.

questions.question:
What is the output of this program?

main :: IO ()
main = do
    print (someFunc 5)

someFunc :: Int -> Int
someFunc x
  | x <= 1 = 1
  | otherwise = x * someFunc (x - 1)
questions.hint: someFunc is a factorial.

questions.question:
What is the output of this program?

main :: IO ()
main = do
    print (someFunc 3)

someFunc :: Int -> Int
someFunc 1 = 1
someFunc n = 2 * someFunc (n - 1) + 1
questions.hint: Unroll it: someFunc 1, then someFunc 2, then someFunc 3.

questions.question:
What is the output of this program?

main :: IO ()
main = print (takeWhile (< 40) (map (^2) [1..]))
questions.hint: map squares the infinite list; takeWhile stops once a square reaches 40.

questions.question:
What is the output of this program?

add :: Int -> Int -> Int
add x y = x + y

main :: IO ()
main = do
    let f = add 3
        g = (* 2) . f
    print (g 4)
questions.hint: g applies f (add 3) first and then multiplies by 2.

questions.question:
What is the output of this program?

main :: IO ()
main = do
    let xs = [1..5]
    print (sum xs * 2)
questions.hint: Add up 1 to 5, then double it.

main = print (map (^2) (filter even [1..5]))

main :: IO ()
main = print (map (^2) (filter odd [1..5]))

main :: IO ()
main = print (map (^2) (filter even [1..6]))

main :: IO ()
main = print (map (*2) (filter even [1..5]))

questions.hint: Evens only, then squared.

questions.question:
Which program produces the following output?

Expected output:
24

choices.statement:
main :: IO ()
main = print (foldr (*) 1 [1..4])

main :: IO ()
main = print (foldr (+) 0 [1..4])

main = print (foldr (*) 0 [1..4])

main = print (foldr (*) 1 [1..5])

questions.hint: 24 is 4!. Try foldr (*) 1.

questions.question:
Which program produces the following output?

Expected output:
[1,2,3]

choices.statement:
main :: IO ()
main = print (take 3 (iterate (+1) 0))

main :: IO ()
main = print (take 3 (iterate (+1) 1))

main = print (take 3 (iterate (*2) 1))

main :: IO ()
main = print (takeWhile (< 3) (iterate (+1) 1))

55

choices.statement:
main :: IO ()
main = print (sum [x * x | x <- [1..5]])

main :: IO ()
main = print (sum [x | x <- [1..5]])

questions.question:
Which program produces the following output?

Expected output:
10

choices.statement:
main :: IO ()
main = print (go 0 1)
  where
    go acc i
      | i > 4 = acc
      | otherwise = go (acc + i) (i + 1)

main :: IO ()
main = print (go 0 1)
  where
    go acc i
      | i > 5 = acc
      | otherwise = go (acc + i) (i + 1)

main :: IO ()
main = print (go 0 1)
  where
    go acc i
      | i > 4 = acc
      | otherwise = go (acc + i) i

main :: IO ()
main = print (go 0 1)
  where
    go acc i
      | i >= 4 = acc
      | otherwise = go (acc + i) (i + 1)

questions.hint: The accumulator adds the numbers 1 through 4.

questions.question:
Which function completes the map call?

Expected output:
[2,4,6]

main :: IO ()
main = print (map __________ [1, 2, 3])
questions.hint: map applies the function to every element: [1,2,3] becomes [2,4,6].

questions.question:
Which expression completes the lambda passed to foldl?

Expected output:
30

main :: IO ()
main = print (foldl (\acc x -> __________) 0 [1, 2, 3, 4])

choices.statement: acc + x
acc + x * x
x * x
acc * x + x

questions.hint: The result is a running sum of squares: 1 + 4 + 9 + 16.

questions.question:
Which expression completes the function composition helper?

Expected output:
11

compose f g x = __________

main :: IO ()
main = print (compose (+ 1) (* 2) 5)

choices.statement: g (f x)
f (g x)
f x + g x
f (g (g x))

questions.hint: compose f g x applies g first, then f.
The function squares its argument.
factorial(4) = 4 x 3 x 2 x 1.
